claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase, uniformly lamellar microstructure.
The baseline lamellar colonies contain numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
A tailored thermomechanical processing intervention can generate a hierarchical architecture with graded lamellar spacing or interpenetrating networks in a eutectic HEA.
Processing conditions can be controlled to refine the lamellae and impose spatial variation in lamellar spacing.
Closely spaced lamellae restrict dislocation motion and enhance strength.
More widely spaced lamellar regions distribute strain more uniformly and delay crack growth.
A graded lamellar architecture blunts or deflects crack propagation along internal boundaries.
A graded lamellar architecture facilitates more uniform strain distribution during tensile loading.
Refined load-bearing paths and suppression of localized stress concentrations increase tensile strength.
Delaying catastrophic microcrack coalescence increases tensile ductility.
The hierarchical architecture will produce higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified uniform-lamellar baseline.
The hierarchical architecture will produce greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the unmodified uniform-lamellar baseline.
The proposed intervention is applicable to eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures.
Significant changes in phase composition or interfacial characteristics may limit the intervention's effectiveness.
The magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement depends on precise control of the graded architecture.
